assessment.Existence of an interference: The applicant’s freedom of expression was interfered with through the initiation of criminal proceedings against her (see paragraph 12), the decision of the Disciplinary Chamber of the Supreme Court (DCSC) to lift her judicial immunity, suspend her from judicial duties, and reduce her salary by 50% (see paragraph 13), as well as the defamatory public statements made by State officials and State-controlled media (see paragraphs 19 and 21). These measures were taken in direct response to the applicant’s public criticism—both in her capacity as President of the Judges’ Association Themis and as an individual judge—of the Government’s judicial reforms and the Minister of Justice (see paragraphs 8, 9 and 17). The European Court of Human Rights has routinely recognised that criminal proceedings, disciplinary sanctions, and State-orchestrated public campaigns can constitute interference with the right to freedom of expression under Article 10 (see no. 28396/95). Therefore, there has been an interference with the applicant’s rights under Article 10 of the Convention.
assessment.Lawfulness of the interference: The interference had a basis in domestic law. The prosecutor’s application to lift the applicant’s immunity was grounded in specific provisions of the Criminal Code (Articles 228 § 3, 231 § 2 and 284 § 2, as cited in paragraph 24), and the DCSC acted pursuant to the applicable national legal framework in lifting her immunity, suspending her, and imposing the salary reduction (see paragraph 13). The Court has consistently held that interference prescribed by domestic law satisfies the ‘lawfulness’ requirement under Article 10 § 2 (see no. 28274/08). Thus, the interference in the present case was lawful.
assessment.Legitimate aims of the interference: The interference pursued legitimate aims as defined in Article 10 § 2. The criminal proceedings were initiated to investigate allegations of abuse of power, misappropriation of public funds, and bribery (see paragraph 12), which fall under the aim of ‘the prevention of crime’. Additionally, the DCSC’s resolution referred to the need to address conduct ‘detrimental to the administration of justice and to the State Treasury’ (see paragraph 13), which aligns with the aims of ‘protecting the rights of others’ and ‘maintaining the authority and impartiality of the judiciary’. The Court has previously accepted such aims as valid justifications for interference (see no. 28396/95). Therefore, the interference pursued legitimate aims.
assessment.Necessary in a democratic society: The interference was not necessary in a democratic society. Firstly, the second-instance decision of the DCSC concluded that the evidence adduced by the prosecutor was insufficient to substantiate the charges, with the main witness’s credibility being ‘diminished’ due to inconsistent testimony (see paragraph 15). This undermines any assertion of a pressing social need for the interference. Secondly, the measures imposed—including a 238-day suspension and a 50% salary reduction (see paragraph 16)—were severe and disproportionate, particularly given that the criminal proceedings were ultimately discontinued (see paragraph 22). Thirdly, the timing of the proceedings, which followed the applicant’s public criticism of the Government (see paragraphs 8, 9 and 17), together with the State-controlled media’s defamatory coverage (see paragraph 19) and the Government officials’ public condemnation of the DCSC’s eventual refusal to lift her immunity (see paragraph 21), strongly suggest that the interference was motivated by a desire to silence her dissent. The Court has emphasised that restrictions on the freedom of expression of judges—who play a vital role in a democratic society—require strict scrutiny and must not produce a chilling effect (see no. 28274/08). Here, the interference not only had a chilling effect (see paragraph 18) but was also conducted by a body (the DCSC) whose legality was contested and whose actions defied a binding order of the Court of Justice of the European Union (see paragraphs 20-21). Consequently, the interference cannot be justified as necessary in a democratic society.
